meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.title: A randomized control trial to establish the feasibility and safety of rapamycin treatment in an older human cohort
data.authors: Kraig E; Linehan LA; Liang H; Romo TQ; Liu Q; et al.; Kellogg DL

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: A safety-first pilot RCT (n=25, ages 70-95) asking the basic question before any longevity trial: is daily rapamycin safe in healthy older people? Over 8+ weeks it was well tolerated with only minor red-blood-cell changes and - importantly - NO rise in blood glucose or insulin resistance in this short window. Groundwork for larger aging trials like PEARL.
data.abstract_excerpt: Inhibition of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway by rapamycin (RAPA), an FDA-approved immunosuppressive drug used as a clinical therapy to prevent solid organ allograft rejection, enhances longevity in mice. Importantly, RAPA was efficacious even when initiated in relatively old animals, suggesting that mTOR inhibition could potentially slow the progression of aging-associated pathologies in older humans (Harrison et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2011). However, the safety and tolerability of RAPA in older human subjects have not yet been demonstrated.

extracted_findings.effect: Well tolerated; NO rise in blood glucose / insulin resistance in the short window – groundwork for larger geroprotection trials
extracted_findings.dose: Rapamycin 1 mg daily orally (single dose tested; blood levels monitored in first 4 subjects), ~8-16 weeks; placebo-controlled.
extracted_findings.sample_size: n=25 randomised (11 rapamycin, 14 placebo analysed); healthy older adults aged 70-95.
extracted_findings.effect_size: Established feasibility and safety of daily low-dose rapamycin in older adults; no serious adverse events; groundwork for larger geroprotection trials.
extracted_findings.limitations: Small sample -> single 1 mg dose chosen; short duration; feasibility (not efficacy) study.
